config.title: Build GitHub user search with pagination

intro.title: Build GitHub user search with pagination
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a GitHub user search application that fetches user data from the GitHub API and displays it with pagination. You will learn how to make HTTP requests to an external API, handle asynchronous data fetching, and manage application state for search results and pagination controls. The main technologies involved are the Fetch API for network requests, async/await for handling promises, and DOM manipulation to update the user interface. By the end, you'll have a functional app that lets users search for GitHub profiles and navigate through pages of results.
intro.usecase: Searching and paginating through large datasets is a core pattern in modern web applications. You'll implement this in dashboards like admin panels to browse users, in e-commerce sites to filter products, or in content platforms to navigate articles. Mastering this skill allows you to build efficient, user-friendly interfaces that handle real data from APIs like GitHub, ensuring smooth performance even with thousands of results.

objectives: Construct a search interface that captures user input and triggers API requests
Implement state management for search results, loading status, and error handling
Configure API calls to GitHub's user search endpoint with dynamic query parameters
Render user data in a responsive grid layout with avatar, username, and profile links
Integrate pagination controls to navigate through multiple pages of search results
Manipulate the DOM to update search results without page refresh
Initialize and control pagination state to track current page and total results

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring React and the useState hook into your file.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are available for use in your component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a function component named App that returns an empty div.
steps.hint: Define a function called App that returns JSX containing a single div element.
steps.seedCode:
// Import React and useState from 'react'

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns an empty div.
successCriteria: A function named App is defined and returns a div element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main App component structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you define a function named App that returns a div element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component isn't defined correctly. Create a function named App that returns a div.

steps.title: Initialize search query state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use useState to create a state variable named 'query' initialized to an empty string.
steps.hint: Call useState with an empty string as the initial value, and destructure the returned array into query and setQuery.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: creating a state variable for input
const [inputValue, setInputValue] = useState('');
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a query state variable ready to store the user's search input.
successCriteria: The App component contains a useState call that creates a 'query' state variable initialized to an empty string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the search query state. This will track what the user types in the search box.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using useState to create a state variable named 'query' with an empty string as the initial value.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Inside the App component, use useState to create a state variable called 'query' that starts as an empty string.

steps.title: Initialize users data state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use useState to create a state variable named 'users' initialized to an empty array.
steps.hint: Call useState with [] as the initial value and destructure the returned array into a variable and setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: state for a list of items
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have a 'users' state variable ready to store fetched GitHub user data.
successCriteria: The component contains a 'users' state variable initialized to an empty array using useState.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the users state. This will hold the GitHub user data we fetch later.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with [] as the initial value and naming the variable 'users'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to add a state variable named 'users' initialized to an empty array using useState.

steps.title: Initialize current page state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use useState to create a state variable named 'page' and initialize it to 1.
steps.hint: Add a new useState call after the existing state declarations. The syntax is similar to the query state you already created.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: creating a state variable for page number
const [page, setPage] = useState(1);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a 'page' state variable initialized to 1, ready to track pagination.
successCriteria: A 'page' state variable is declared with useState and initialized to 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the page state. This will help track which page of search results we're on.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState to create a state variable named 'page' with an initial value of 1.
steps.feedbackWrong: The page state wasn't properly initialized. You need to add a useState call for 'page' with initial value 1.

steps.title: Define search handler function
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define an async function named handleSearch that will fetch users from the GitHub API. The function should take no parameters for now.
steps.hint: Write an async function that uses the fetch API. You'll add the implementation in later steps.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component now contains an async handleSearch function that will later fetch GitHub users.
successCriteria: An async function named handleSearch is defined inside the App component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the handleSearch function. This will be the core function that fetches data from GitHub's API.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've defined an async function named handleSearch inside your App component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleSearch function isn't properly defined. Check that it's an async function inside your App component.

steps.title: Add search input field
steps.instruction: Add an input element inside the div with type='text', value bound to the query state, and an onChange handler that updates the query state.
steps.hint: Use the setQuery function from useState to update the query state when the input changes.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: input field with state binding
<input type="text" value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} />
steps.expectedOutcome: The input field will appear below the heading, and typing in it will update the query state.
successCriteria: An input element with type='text', value={query}, and onChange handler that calls setQuery is added to the JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the search input field with proper state binding.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added an input, but check that it has type='text', value={query}, and an onChange handler that calls setQuery.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input field is missing or incorrect. Make sure to add an input element with the required attributes and event handler.

steps.title: Add search button and wire click handler
steps.instruction: Add a button element with the text 'Search' inside the return statement, and set its onClick prop to call the handleSearch function.
steps.hint: Place the button after the input field. Use the onClick event handler to trigger the handleSearch function when the button is clicked.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a button with a click handler
<button onClick={handleClick}>Submit</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Search' appears below the input field, and clicking it will trigger the search handler.
successCriteria: A button element with text 'Search' is added, and its onClick prop is set to handleSearch.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the search button and wired it to the handler. Now users can trigger the search by clicking the button.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but make sure it has the text 'Search' and the onClick prop is set to handleSearch.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or not correctly wired. Add a button element with text 'Search' and set onClick={handleSearch}.

steps.title: Display users list
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add a list that maps through the users state array and displays each user's login name.
steps.hint: Use the map method on the users array to generate list items. Each list item should display the user's login property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a list structure ready to display GitHub users when the users state contains data.
successCriteria: A map function is used on the users array to generate list items, each displaying a user's login name.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the list structure to display GitHub users.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some list structure, but make sure you're using the map method on the users array and displaying the login property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The list structure for displaying users isn't implemented correctly. Review how to map through arrays in JSX.

steps.title: Add previous page button
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add a button with the text 'Previous' that decrements the current page state when clicked.
steps.hint: You'll need to add a button element with an onClick handler that calls a function to decrease the page number. Use the setCurrentPage function to update the state.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: button that decrements a counter
<button onClick={() => setCount(count - 1)}>Decrease</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A 'Previous' button appears in the UI that, when clicked, will decrease the current page number.
successCriteria: The button has the text 'Previous' and an onClick handler that decrements the currentPage state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the Previous button with proper click handling to navigate back through pages.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but make sure it has the correct text and properly decrements the currentPage state when clicked.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Previous button is missing or doesn't properly handle click events to decrement the page number.

steps.title: Add next page button
steps.instruction: Add a 'Next' button after the previous page button that increments the currentPage state when clicked.
steps.hint: Create a button element with text 'Next' and an onClick handler that calls setCurrentPage with currentPage + 1.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: button that increments a counter
<button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Increment</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A 'Next' button appears after the previous page button that increases the page number when clicked.
successCriteria: A button with text 'Next' is added with an onClick handler that increments currentPage.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the next page button. This completes the pagination navigation UI.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but make sure it has the correct text 'Next' and properly increments currentPage when clicked.
steps.feedbackWrong: The next page button is missing or incorrect. Add a button with text 'Next' that increments currentPage when clicked.

steps.title: Update search handler with pagination
steps.instruction: Modify the handleSearch function to include the currentPage state in the GitHub API URL when fetching users.
steps.hint: Update the fetch URL to include '&page=' followed by the currentPage value. The GitHub API uses query parameters for pagination.
steps.expectedOutcome: The handleSearch function will be updated to fetch users for the current page from the GitHub API.
successCriteria: The handleSearch function includes the currentPage variable in the fetch URL to enable paginated searches.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully integrated pagination into the search handler. The API will now fetch users for the correct page.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the fetch URL includes the currentPage parameter. Check if you're using template literals correctly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleSearch function still needs to be updated. Remember to include the currentPage state in the GitHub API URL.
